analysis.one_liner: Protects millions of acres of Northern Rockies public land as wilderness and bans new road building, logging, mining, and drilling there.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 45 House cosponsors, all Democrats, but never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have permanently protected a connected stretch of wild federal land across Idaho, Montana, Oregon, Washington, and Wyoming. It would designate millions of acres of National Forest, National Park, and Bureau of Land Management land as wilderness, protect certain rivers under the Wild and Scenic Rivers System, and connect the protected cores with wildlife corridors. After scientists evaluated remaining roadless areas, no new road construction, timber cutting, mining, or oil and gas leasing would be allowed there without another act of Congress. The bill also would fund restoration work on already-damaged tracts, which its sponsors argued would create jobs for local contractors.
analysis.who_benefits: People who hunt, fish, hike, and recreate on Northern Rockies public lands keep those landscapes intact and free of new roads and development. Downstream communities get cleaner, cheaper water from protected headwaters of the Columbia, Snake, Missouri, and other river systems. Local businesses would be in line for restoration contracts to repair damaged tracts. Wildlife — including grizzly bears, wolves, and endangered fish — would keep connected habitat corridors across the bioregion.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hunters, anglers, hikers, and public-lands users

how_it_helps.text: Designates millions of acres of National Forest, National Park, and Bureau of Land Management lands in Idaho, Montana, Oregon, Washington, and Wyoming as wilderness — including lands in the Greater Yellowstone, Greater Glacier, Greater Hells Canyon, and Greater Salmon/Selway ecosystems — keeping them open to hunting, fishing, hiking, and other non-motorized recreation.

Protects the headwaters of the Columbia, Snake, Missouri, Green, and Saskatchewan river systems, which the bill says would cut water treatment and irrigation costs and support farming, ranching, and water-based recreation downstream.

After an evaluation by a panel of independent scientists, it bars new road construction, timber harvest, mining, and oil and gas leasing on roadless lands larger than 1,000 acres unless Congress specifically votes to allow it.

Creates wildland recovery areas and requires federal agencies to write restoration plans for damaged tracts — such as clear-cuts near the Yellowstone boundary — and the bill's findings argue this work would be contracted to local businesses, creating jobs in outdoor trades.
Links the protected core ecosystems with biological connecting corridors so large animals like grizzly bears, wolves, and elk can move between habitats as the climate changes.

analysis.who_pays: Timber companies lose access to roadless federal forest land for logging and road building. Mining and oil and gas companies lose access to areas they could otherwise lease and develop. Some rural communities in Idaho, Montana, and Wyoming that have historically depended on timber jobs could bear the adjustment cost, and the bill bars motorized recreation in designated wilderness, which affects snowmobilers and off-road riders.
analysis.who_pays_short: Timber, mining, and oil and gas firms

drawbacks.text: Wilderness designation permanently bars road construction and timber harvest on the designated lands, which opponents said would cost logging jobs in rural communities in Idaho, Montana, and Wyoming that have historically depended on timber work.

The restrictions are permanent by design: after the scientific evaluation, no new road building, timber cutting, mining, or oil and gas leasing is allowed on the covered roadless lands without a new act of Congress, so future decisions about those lands would be taken away from agencies and local planning processes.
Wilderness under the Wilderness Act is closed to motorized recreation, so snowmobilers, off-road vehicle riders, and some outfitters who use these areas today would lose access.

The bill acknowledges that rural resource-dependent communities in the region already face economic instability and high unemployment, so adding restrictions on extraction carries real risk for towns with few alternative employers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded permanent protection of a large, intact wild ecosystem — with its clean water, wildlife habitat, and recreation economy — for restrictions on timber, mining, and energy development on those specific federal lands. The strongest objection is real: some rural communities in the region have historically depended on logging work, and wilderness designations cannot be undone without another act of Congress, so the choice is effectively irreversible. The bill's own answer — that below-cost timber sales already cost taxpayers money and that restoration contracts would replace some logging jobs — is plausible but unproven, and it is uncertain how many jobs restoration work would actually create. For most Americans, whose stake in these lands is as citizens and recreation users rather than as extraction companies, the protection side of the ledger outweighs the cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Natural Resources Committee, which passed it along to a subcommittee, where it sat for the rest of the two-year Congress without ever being debated or voted on, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Carolyn Maloney of New York introduced the Northern Rockies Ecosystem Protection Act on February 22, 2019, with 21 original cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
On March 7, 2019, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on National Parks, Forests, and Public Lands — and no further action was ever taken on it.

It eventually gathered 44 cosponsors, every one of them a House Democrat, and none of the bill's supporters sat on the committee with jurisdiction in a way that changed its fate; even with Democrats holding the House majority and chairing the Natural Resources Committee, the bill never got a markup or a floor vote.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, so under House rules the bill expired and would have had to be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Timber, mining, and oil and gas interests that operate on Northern Rockies federal lands are better off, because the roadless acres stayed open to road building, timber sales, and mineral leasing. Off-road and motorized recreation users also kept the access they have today, while people who wanted the land permanently protected got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Timber, mining, and oil and gas firms

for.name: Carolyn B. Maloney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 22, 2019 and led it through the Congress; it never advanced past subcommittee referral.

for.name: 44 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Democrat, and no Republican signed on.

against.name: Timber, mining, and oil and gas interests in the Northern Rockies
against.role: Extractive industries with access to federal lands in Idaho, Montana, Wyoming, Oregon, and Washington
against.what_they_did: Have long opposed wilderness designations and roadless-area protections that would close federal lands to logging and mineral development; the bill died in committee without ever reaching a vote, so their access to these lands was never restricted.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee and its National Parks, Forests, and Public Lands Subcommittee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (chaired by Rep. Raúl Grijalva, D-AZ)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittee on March 7, 2019 and took no further action on it for the remainder of the Congress; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred.

sides.party_line_note: All 45 supporters in the House — the sponsor and 44 cosponsors — were Democrats, with no Republican cosponsor; because the bill never came to a vote, no roll call exists to show how the full chamber would have split.

industries.note: The bill ends road building and timber harvest on the covered roadless lands and designated wilderness, removing timber supply that logging companies and rural mills draw from federal forests in the Northern Rockies. The bill's findings argue many of these sales are below-cost — taxpayers subsidize them — and that restoration work would replace some of the jobs.

Wilderness designation and the roadless-lands ban prohibit mineral leasing, mining, and drilling that would impair the land's natural character, closing areas these companies could otherwise bid on. The industry loses access to federal lands that are currently open to development.

Guides, outfitters, and gateway communities depend on hunting, fishing, and backcountry recreation; permanently protecting the landscapes and the fisheries at the headwaters of major rivers protects the base of that economy. The bill's findings describe these lands as among the most popular wild lands in the country.

The bill directs agencies to develop recovery plans for damaged wildland areas and says rehabilitation projects would be contracted to local businesses, creating work restoring roads, streams, and clear-cuts.
